Quotquot autem receperunt eum: dedit eis potestatem filios dei fieri: his qui credunt in nomine eius. Qui non ex sanguinibus neque ex voluntate carnis: neque ex voluntate viri: sed ex deo nati sunt. Et verbum caro factum est et habitavit in nobis. Et vidimus gloriam eius. gloriam quasi unigeniti a patre: plenum gratiae et veritatis. Hoc totum quod ex evangelio posui: in precedentibus suis partibus quod immutabile ac sempiternum est: cuius contemplatio nos beatos facit. In sequentibus vero: mixta cum temporalibus commemorant eterna. Ac per hoc aliqua ibi ad scientiam pertinent: aliqua ad sapientiam: sicut libro duodecimo processu nostra distinctio. Nam in principio erat verbum: et verbum erat apud deum: et deus erat verbum: hoc erat in principio apud deum omnia per ipsum facta sunt: et sine ipso factum est nihil: quod factum est in ipso vita erat: et vita erat lux hominum et lux in tenebris lucet: et tenebrae eam non comprehenderunt. Contemplativam vita requirit: et intellectuali mente cernendum est. Qua in re quanto magis quisque profecerit: tanto fiet sine dubitatione sapientior. Sed propter id quod ait. Lux lucet in tenebris: et tenebrae eam non comprehenderunt: fide utique opus erat qua crederetur quod non videt. Tenebras quippe intelligi voluit aversa ab huius luce caecisque minus idonea ad tueri corda mortalium. propter quod adiungitur et dicit. Fuit homo missus a deo: cui nomen erat iohannes: hic venit in testimonium ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine ut omnes crederent per illum. Hoc tam temporaliter gestum est: et ad scientiam pertinet quae cognitione historica continetur. Hominem autem iohannem in phantasia cogitamus: quia de humanae naturae noticia impressa est nostrae memoriae. Et hoc eodem modo cogitat sive qui ista non credit: sive qui credit. Utrumque enim notum est quid sit homo. cuius exteriore parte id est corpore per corporis lumina didicerunt. Interiore vero. id est animam in semetipsis: quia et ipsi homines sunt: et per humanam conversationem cognitam tenent: ut possint cogitare quod dicitur. Fuit homo cui nomen erat iohannes: quia et nomina sciunt loquendo et audiendo. Quod autem ibi est: missus a deo: fide tenent qui tenent. Et qui fide non tenent: aut dubitatione ambigunt aut infidelitate derident. Utrique tamen si non

Si quidem porro ipsam quam videt quisque in corde suo si credit. vel non esse: si non credit. aliter novimus: non sicut corpora quae videmus oculis corporis: et per ipsorum imagines quas memoria tenemus: etiam absentia cogitamus nec sicut ea quae non vidimus et ex his quae vidimus cogitatione utcunque formamus: et memoriae commendamus: quo recurramus cum voluerimus: ut illic ea vel potius qualescunque imagines eorum quas ibi fiximus similiter recordatione cernamus. Nec sicut hominem vivum cuius animam etiam si non videmus ex nostra coniicimus: et ex motibus corporalibus hominem vivum. sicut vivendo didicimus intuemur etiam cogitando. Non sic videtur fides in corde in quo est ab eo cuius est: sed eam tenet certissima scientia: clamatque conscientia. Cum itaque propterea credere iubeamur quia id quod credere iubemur videre non possumus. ipsam tamen fidem quando inest in nobis videmus in nobis: quia et rerum absentium praesens est fides: et rerum quae foris sunt intus est fides. et rerum quae non videntur videtur fides: et ipsa tamen temporaliter fit in cordibus hominum. Et si ex infidelibus fideles fiunt: perit ab eis. Aliquando autem et rebus falsis accomodatur fides. loquimur enim sic ut dicamus habita est ei fides et decepit. Qualis fides: si tamen et ipsa dicenda est fides non culpabiliter de cordibus perit: quando eam inventa veritas pellit optabiliter autem rerum verarum in easdem res fides transit. Non enim dicendum est perit: quando ea quae credebantur videntur. Nunquid enim adhuc fides dicenda est cum diffinita sit in epistola ad hebreos fides: dictumque sit eam esse convictio neque rerum quae non videntur. Deinde quod sequitur. He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him. But as many as received him, to them he gave the power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name; who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth. <note>John 1:9–14.</note> All of this which I have set down from the Gospel pertains in its preceding parts to what is immutable and eternal, the contemplation of which makes us blessed. In its following parts, however, eternal things are recalled mingled with temporal things. And by this, certain things there belong to <term>scientia</term> <gloss>temporal knowledge</gloss>, and certain things to <term>sapientia</term> <gloss>eternal wisdom</gloss>, just as our distinction proceeded in the twelfth book. For "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; the same was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him, and without him was made nothing; that which was made in him was life, and the life was the light of men; and the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it" <note>John 1:1–5.</note> requires a contemplative life, and must be discerned by the intellectual mind. In this matter, the more one advances, the wiser without doubt one will become. But because he says, "The light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it," there was certainly need of faith by which that which is not seen might be believed. For by "darkness" he wished to be understood the hearts of mortals turned away from this light and blind, less suited for gazing upon it. On account of this it is added and he says: "There was a man sent from God, whose name was John; this man came for a witness, to bear witness concerning the light, that all might believe through him." <note>John 1:6–7.</note> This was enacted in a temporal manner, and pertains to knowledge which is contained in historical awareness. Now, we conceive the man John in our imagination, because the knowledge of human nature is imprinted on our memory. And both he who does not believe these things and he who believes thinks in this same way. For to both it is known what a man is. Its exterior part, that is, the body, they have learned through the eyes of the body; the interior part, however, that is, the soul, in themselves, because they too are human beings, and through human fellowship they hold it as known, so that they are able to think what is said: "There was a man whose name was John," because they also know names by speaking and hearing. But as to what is there, "sent by God," those who hold it hold it by faith. And those who do not hold it by faith either waver in doubt or mock in unbelief. Yet both, if they
<column-break/>
are not of the number of the exceedingly foolish, who says in his heart "There is no God," <note>Psalm 14:1.</note> upon hearing these words each one considers both what God is and what it is to be sent by God; and if not as the reality is, certainly according to their capacity. Furthermore, we know faith itself, which each person sees in his own heart if he believes, or sees not to be there if he does not believe, in another way: not like bodies which we see with the eyes of the body, and through their images which we retain in memory we imagine even when absent; nor like those things which we have not seen and in some way shape in thought from those things which we have seen, and commit to memory, to which we may return when we wish, so that there we may similarly discern by recollection them, or rather whatever images of them we fixed there. Nor is it like a living man, whose soul, even if we do not see it, we infer from our own, and from bodily movements perceive a living man, just as we have learned by living, even in our thought. Not in this way is faith seen in the heart in which it exists by the one whose faith it is; but most certain knowledge holds it, and conscience proclaims it. Since therefore we are commanded to believe for the reason that we cannot see that which we are commanded to believe, nevertheless when faith is within us, we see faith itself within us: because faith is the presence of absent things, and faith is the interior reality of things that are outside, and faith is seen of things that are not seen; and yet it comes to be temporally in the hearts of human beings. And if from unbelievers they become believers, it passes away from them. At times, however, faith is also extended to false things; for we speak in such a way as to say "faith was placed in him, and he deceived." Such faith, if indeed it should be called faith, departs from hearts without blame when discovered truth drives it out; but desirably the faith of true things passes over into those very things. For it should not be said to perish when those things which were believed are seen. For should it still be called faith, when faith has been defined in the Epistle to the Hebrews, and it was said to be the conviction of things that are not seen? <note>Hebrews 11:1.</note> Then that which follows: "He came for a witness, to bear witness concerning the light, that all might believe through him" is, as I have said, a temporal action. For in a temporal manner he bears witness even concerning an eternal thing, which is the intelligible light. In detta provincia di Maabar gli abitanti sono negri ⁸⁴⁶, ma non nascono così com' essi si fanno con artifizio, perchè reputano la negrezza per gran beltà. E però ogni giorno ungono li fanciullini tre volte con olio di susimani ⁸⁴⁷. Gli idolatri di questa provincia fanno le immagini de' loro idoli tutte nere, e dipingono il diavolo bianco ⁸⁴⁸, dicendo, che tutti li demoni sono bianchi. E quelli che adorano il bue, come vanno a combattere portano seco del pelo del bue salvatico ⁸⁴⁹, e li cavalieri legano del detto pelo ai crini del cavallo, tenendolo che sia di tanta santità, e virtù, che ciascuno che n' ha sopra di se, sia sicuro da ogni pericolo. E per questa causa i peli de' buoi salvatichi vagliono assai denari in quelle parti.

846. *Gli abitanti sono negri.* Il colore dei Malabari é oscuro dice il P. Paolino (l. c. p. 111) > ma assai più chiaro dei *Tamuli* cioè degli abitanti della costa Ciolemandola (e di questi appunto parla il Polo). I pescatori o *Mucuas*, i *Paravas* gente addetta alla tessitura, e tintura delle tele colle quali traffica, e gli altri abitanti della spiaggia del mare sono negri, perchè più esposti al sole ed all' aria marina, che tinge il volto di color nero. Le tribù nobili, ed alcune altre famiglie che abitano li palmeti, le foreste, le montagne, e sulle rive dei fiumi sono assai bianche <. Dice il Barbosa: > la gente é negra, bruna, e berrettina < (apud Ram. p. 366).

847. *Ungono li fanciulli con olio di susimani* (V. t. I. p. 180 n. c).

848. *Immagini de' loro idoli tutte nere e il diavolo bianco.* Fra le immagini delle tanto fantastiche divinità dell' India fatte incidere dal P. Paolino nel suo Sistema Bramanico, non vedesi rappresentato in nero che *Vishnu* nella sua pretesa prima e seconda incarnazione (Tab. VIII et IX). Tratto da una pittura Indica del Museo Borgiano vedesi questo nume circondato da mali genj di color bianco che il Polo potè crederli demonj vedendovisi effigiati come si suole effigiare i diavoli fra noi. Il dotto Missionario dice: > malos genios, quos daemones vocant, clari Brahmanes cum tota antiquitate docent <, ed ei discorre delle varie opinioni degl' Indiani intorno a quei genj malefici. I loro idoli che sono di bronzo, o di basalte ch'è il marmo degli Indiani (Paul a S Bartolom. Viag. p. 49), s' annerano anche più col fumo delle lampade. In the said province of <term>Maabar</term> <gloss>Coromandel coast</gloss> the inhabitants are dark <note>note 846</note>, but they are not born as dark as they make themselves by artifice, because they consider blackness a great beauty. For this reason, every day they anoint young children three times with sesame oil <note>note 847</note>. The idolaters of this province make the images of their idols entirely black, and they paint the devil white <note>note 848</note>, saying that all demons are white. And those who worship the ox, when they go into battle, carry with them hair of the wild ox <note>note 849; the wild yak</note>, and the horsemen tie some of this hair to the horse's mane, holding it to possess such holiness and virtue that anyone who carries it upon himself is safe from all danger. For this reason, the hair of wild oxen is worth a great deal of money in those regions.

---

846. *The inhabitants are black.* The color of the Malabar people is dark, says Father Paolino <note>loco citato, page 111</note>, but much lighter than the Tamils, that is, the inhabitants of the Coromandel Coast <note>and Polo is speaking precisely of these</note>. The fishermen or <term>Mukkuvar</term> <gloss>coastal fishing caste</gloss>, the <term>Paravas</term> <gloss>coastal merchant and diving caste</gloss> people dedicated to weaving and dyeing fabrics in which they trade, and the other inhabitants of the seashore are dark, because they are more exposed to the sun and sea air, which darkens the complexion. The noble castes and some other families who dwell in the palm groves, forests, mountains, and along the riverbanks are quite fair. Barbosa says: "the people are black, brown, and tawny" <note>in Ramusio, page 366</note>.

847. *They anoint children with sesame oil* <note>See volume I, page 180, note c</note>.

848. *Images of their idols entirely black and the devil white.* Among the images of the many fanciful deities of India engraved by order of Father Paolino in his *Brahmanical System*, only Vishnu in his alleged first and second incarnations is represented in black <note>Plates VIII and IX</note>. Drawn from an Indian painting in the Borgia Museum, this divinity is seen surrounded by white malevolent spirits, which Polo could have thought to be demons upon seeing them depicted as devils are typically depicted among us. The learned missionary says: "the distinguished Brahmins along with all antiquity teach that there are evil spirits, which they call demons" <note>original Latin: "malos genios, quos daemones vocant, clari Brahmanes cum tota antiquitate docent"</note>, and he discusses the various opinions of the Indians concerning those maleficent spirits. Their idols, which are made of bronze or basalt, which is the marble of the Indians <note>Paolino da San Bartolomeo, *Travels*, page 49</note>, become even blacker from the smoke of lamps. The missionary describes the frightening manner in which they depict <term>Ciardhava</term> <gloss>fire-breathing deity</gloss>, or the fire-spitting deity <note>page 26</note>; and Varthema describes the frightening idol of the King of Calicut called <term>Deumo</term> <gloss>demon</gloss> <note>Ramusio, volume I, page 174</note>.

849. *Hair of the wild ox.* Father Paolino recounts that the Indians hold similar superstitions regarding the cow's tail <note>*Brahmanical System*, page 202</note>: "When swearing oaths, the pagans bind themselves by an oath by touching the tail of a cow; when they are near death they seize the cow's tail, wishing to be carried by it into heaven, that is, they believe they lead their soul by transmigration into the cow while expiring as they touch its tail" <note>original Latin: "Gentiles dum jurant, vaccae caudam tangendo, jure jurando se obstringunt, dum morti proximi sunt caudam vaccae arripiunt, et ea in coelum vehi volunt, id est animam transmigratione in vaccam inducere se putant, dum caudam ejus tangendo expirant"</note>.

<summary>Marco Polo describes customs in the province of Maabar, including darkening children with sesame oil, depicting deities in black and demons in white, and carrying sacred wild ox hair for protection in battle, accompanied by nineteenth-century editorial commentary on South Indian ethnography and religion.</summary>

### Gen.—Bassia.

*Sp. Bassia longifolia*, (Illupei tree,) *Roxb. Fl. Ind.* ii. p. 523.

The fruit by expression yields a large quantity of oil, much used in India.

*B. butyracea*, *As. Res.* viii. 477. Fulwa, or Phulwara of Nepal and Almora.

*B. latifolia*, Madooka, *Sans.* (Mowa tree, Roxburgh) both yield oil abundantly.

The petals of the Mowa contain sugar, and are much used for the manufacture of a very intoxicating spirit.

The products of the Bassia trees deserve further investigation. The Fulwa butter is a soft solid at 95°.

### NAT. ORDER LXXXVI.—EBENACEÆ.

Trees devoid of milky juice or resin, with alternate, entire, often coriaceous and shining leaves, flowers solitary or united at the axillæ of the leaves, the central system of the stem is coloured, of a deep black.

### Gen.—Diospyros.

*Sp.* 1. *Diospyros Embryopteris*.
*Syn.* Embryopteris glutinifera. *D. glutinosa*, *Kön.*
*Vern.* Sindica, *Sans.* Gaub, *Hind.* and *Bengalee*. Jumika, *Tel.* Toombikai, *Tamul*.

Fruit about two inches in diameter, green when ripe, and farinaceous externally. On being pressed, an excessively astringent juice exudes. This is so powerful that it generally yields on analysis 60 per 100 of pure tannic acid. It is used in medicine as a valuable astringent and styptic, and is employed in Bengal for paying the bottoms of boats. The bark has been given with doubtful results in the treatment of intermittent fevers. See "*Extracts*," Pharmacopœia.

*Sp.* 2. *D. Melanoxylon*, ebony tree.
*Vern.* Kendoo, *Beng.*
Coromandel, Malabar, Ceylon, Midnapore jungles. Bark astringent, given by the native doctors with pepper in dysentery.

*Sp.* 3. *D. virginiana*. United States. Bark said to be powerfully astringent.

<term>عَنْ</term> <gloss>‘an</gloss>. It is said: <term>عَن خمسين فرسخًا من عمان</term>, <gloss>*at a distance of fifty parasangs from Oman*</gloss>, <note>al-Hamadhānī</note> 7, 14; <term>عن قرب مسافة ما بين العدوتين</term>, <gloss>*with the smallest interval intervening between the two banks*</gloss>, <note>al-Hamadhānī</note> 7r, 10. It has the same meaning as the English *off* <note>original Latin: "ex adverso, e regione"</note> <gloss>opposite, facing</gloss>, for example, <note>al-Muqaddasī</note> 2, 5: <term>ثم عن جزيرة الصّلاب مضيق</term> <gloss>then off the island of al-Ṣillāb there is a strait</gloss> <note>original Latin: "deinde ex adverso insulae aç-Çilâb sunt angustiae"</note>; al-Mas‘ūdī, I, 263 penultimate line: <term>الجبل الاقرع عن اعمال انطاكية</term> <gloss>Mount al-Aqra‘ facing the districts of Antioch</gloss> <note>original Latin: "e regione agri Antiocheni"</note>. Compare also Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, IV, 137: <term>لا ينزل احد عن المرسى إلّا باذنهم</term> <gloss>no one lands away from the harbor except with their permission</gloss>. From the sense of *rate* or *proportion* <note>original Latin: "ratione"</note> in this phrase: <term>عن صرف سبعة عشر بدينار</term>, <gloss>*at the exchange rate of seventeen dirhams to a dinar*</gloss>, <note>al-Hamadhānī</note> 74, 4.

<term>عِنَب</term> <gloss>‘inab: grape</gloss>. <term>وَقْتُ العِنَبِ</term> <gloss>the grape harvest season</gloss> <note>original Latin: "tempus vindemiae"</note>, opposite to <term>وقت المطر</term> <gloss>the rainy season</gloss>, <note>al-Muqaddasī</note> 425, 11.

<term>عَنَزَرُوت</term> <gloss>‘anazarūt</gloss>, as in Pliny <term>sarcocolla</term> <gloss>flesh-glue</gloss>, designates both the gum and the plant, <note>al-Muqaddasī</note> 420, 10; 443, 9 and following. It is mostly written <term>انزروت</term> <gloss>anzarūt</gloss>, for example, Ibn Jazlah: <term>انزروت هو صمغ شجرة — بجبال فارس واللورجان</term> <gloss>anzarūt is the resin of a tree... in the mountains of Fārs and al-Lūrjān</gloss>. Compare Polak, II, 285.

<term>عَنَفَ</term> <gloss>‘anafa</gloss>. <term>عَنَافَةٌ</term> <gloss>‘anāfah</gloss>, properly a verbal noun, *harshness*, *violence* <note>original Latin: "durities, violentia"</note>, <note>al-Muqaddasī</note> 243 <note>line p</note>, where in the text appears <margin><term>غشامة</term> <gloss>injustice, tyranny</gloss>.</margin>

<term>عَنَق</term> <gloss>‘anaq</gloss>. <term>عُنُقٌ</term> <gloss>‘unuq: neck</gloss>, plural <term>اعناقٌ</term> <gloss>a‘nāq</gloss>, said of fruits of the gourd and pome kind, as explained in the Glossary to al-Idrīsī. It is said: <term>سفرجل باعناق</term> <gloss>quinces with necks</gloss>, <note>al-Hamadhānī</note> 52, 11, *Journal asiatique*, XV, 1, page 121; and <term>سفرجل مُعَنَّقٌ</term> <gloss>necked quinces</gloss>, <note>al-Hamadhānī</note> 52, 22; 60, 5; 64, 12. Hence <term>معنّقة</term> <gloss>mu‘annaqah</gloss> is the *quince* <note>original Latin: "malum cydonium"</note>, <note>al-Muqaddasī</note> 7, 1; 169, 5; 181, 3, 8 and note <note>f</note>. It is said: <term>خرج الناس اليهم عنقًا واحدًا</term> <gloss>the people went out against them in a single column</gloss>, <note>al-Muqaddasī</note> 244 <note>line b</note>.

<term>عنى</term> <gloss>‘anā</gloss> Form II, of a laxative medicine, *moved*, *stimulated the bowels* <note>original Latin: "movit, sollicitavit alvum"</note>, <note>al-Muqaddasī</note> 444, 3 and 4 <note>tashdīd in Manuscript B</note>. Form V with <term>الى</term> <gloss>ilā</gloss>, *undertook a difficult journey* <note>original Latin: "difficile iter suscepit"</note>, <note>al-Muqaddasī</note> 236, 12.

<term>عَهِدَ</term> <gloss>‘ahida</gloss> Form V, *cared for someone*, *looked after someone*: <term>تحت ظلّه وتعهُّده</term>, <gloss>*under his protection and care*</gloss> <note>original Latin: "sub umbra et in tutela eius"</note>, <note>al-Muqaddasī</note> 314 <note>line b</note>, Glossary of Fragments in Dozy. Form VI, the same: <term>تحت كنفه وتَعاهُدِه</term> <gloss>under his wing and care</gloss> <note>original Latin: "in beneficiis et cura"</note>, <note>al-Muqaddasī</note> 148, 1; <term>في اجراء وتعاهد</term> <gloss>in providing sustenance and care</gloss>, <note>al-Muqaddasī</note> 147, 14; 314; 361 <note>line e</note>. With the accusative of the person and <term>ب</term> <gloss>bi-</gloss> of the thing, *he constantly sent something to someone*, <note>al-Hamadhānī</note> 279, 21, Dozy.

<term>عَاجٍ</term> <gloss>‘ājin</gloss>, <term>عَوِجَ</term> <gloss>‘awija</gloss>. *One who works or sells ivory* <note>original Latin: "qui ebur tractat venditve"</note>, <note>al-Iṣṭakhrī</note> 174, 3; <note>al-Hamadhānī</note> 229, 2.

<term>عَود</term> <gloss>‘awd</gloss> Form I with <term>الى</term> <gloss>ilā</gloss>, *pertained to*, *belonged to* <note>original Latin: "pertinuit ad"</note>, <note>al-Iṣṭakhrī</note> 2, last line <note>al-Hamadhānī 4, 14 has yufradu in place of ya‘ūdu</note>.

This is the shortest Act in the play containing only one incident; but it is an important one; it is the accidental friendship between Charudatta and Aryaka.

P. 244. वणिज इव &c.—Similarly Kalidasa compares mountains to merchants in Vik. IV. 4 (धारासारोपनयनपरा नैगमाः सानुमन्तः). शुल्कं—the tax or toll due to the king; घटादिदेयं शुल्कोऽस्त्री । Amara. The bees gathering honey are here compared to men collecting taxes, but it is not a happy simile; toll is not collected from every article for sale. अक्षः—The axle. परिवर्तनं—change (of the axle, *i. e.* putting in another). छिद्रोऽद्य वा—This cannot cause any perceptible delay. वर्त्मान्तो०—कर्मान्तो० *v. l.* left on the road at the close of the work (repair of the road &c.), is preferable to वर्त्मान्तो०, where अन्त has to be taken in the sense of मध्ये ‘in the middle,’ which is rather forced. स्वैरं—easily, as he lists. गुप्तार्यक०—गुप्तः आर्यकः यस्मिंस्तत्प्रवहणम्.

सावशेषापसारः—whose escape is incomplete, yet to be fully effected. साधोस्तु याने—The fact that the carriage belonged to a good man, who would never betray him, is, however, assuring to him. परभृत इव &c.—The simile refers to the habit of the cuckoos to get their eggs hatched by crows. *Cf.* Sak. स्वमपत्यजातमन्यैर्द्विजैः परभृताः खलु पोषयन्ति । V. 22.

Fifthly, I pray that no person will think that I thus write to retaliate Micron's writing. O, no. I leave wrath to him who is judge of all the world. Having summoned to himself the sick men whom we said had been left behind, the chieftain whose territory lay midway along the direct route, named Bononiama, received them kindly as they passed through. He gave them twenty pounds of pure worked gold and supplied an abundance of edible provisions. Nor did he ever wish to leave our men until he had conducted them from his own residence into Pacra. Holding each one by the right hand, he handed them over to Vasco <note>Vasco Núñez de Balboa</note> in person like a faithful trust, saying: "Behold your fellow soldiers, most valiant man! Behold, as my court received them when they arrived, so I return them to you. I could wish they were in better health, but he who hurls thunderbolts and lightnings against wicked men, and who out of his goodness grants us <term>yucca</term> <gloss>cassava root</gloss> and maize through the mildness of the seasons, will repay you and your companions." As he said this, directing his eyes toward heaven, he alluded to the sun. "By crushing our violent and arrogant enemies, you bring peace of mind to us and to our homes. You subdue monsters. We consider that you and your companions, men outstanding in courage, have been sent from on high, so that under the protection of your <term>macana</term> <gloss>wooden sword or war club</gloss> we may live our lives without fear. We shall give everlasting thanks to the Giver of good things for this great happiness brought to us." The interpreters reported that Bononiama the chieftain delivered an address in these and similar words. Vasco returned equal thanks to him for his escort and generosity toward our men; indeed, he honored Bononiama with many gifts highly prized among them. 

Vasco writes that he learned many things from this chieftain concerning the wealth of those regions, which he says he wishes to pass over for the present, deferring them until the event itself. What this cryptic hyperbole means, I do not understand. He seems to promise great things, nor should it be judged unreasonable from his promise that immense riches may be hoped for from there, seeing that they entered no house of the inhabitants in which they did not find gold breastplates or pectorals, or gold necklaces for the neck or arms. 

I make a conjecture from our own houses. If someone, spurred by a craving for iron, were to march with an armed force into Italy or Spain, what iron would he find in the houses? There an iron frying pan, elsewhere an iron cooking pot and trivets set by the fire: an accumulated supply for kitchen necessity. Nowhere will he find anything made of iron that is not fitted for practical use, nor will he obtain a great abundance of iron. That iron exists in those regions would be conjectured from what was found. Our men perceived that those native inhabitants value unworked gold no more than our people value crude iron. 

These things, Blessed Father <note>addressed to Pope Leo X</note>, I hold from the letters and living voice of Vasco Núñez and his fellow soldiers concerning those matters; yet time, which reveals all hidden things, will disclose them more clearly. They were unable to achieve anything remarkable in searching out gold mines, because out of the one hundred and ninety men whom we mentioned Vasco had led out from Darién, he used the labor of only seventy, or at most eighty, in conducting operations. The rest were always left behind in the houses of the chieftains. But he says that those who had recently been brought from Hispaniola fell especially into various illnesses. These men, certainly, could not endure such hardship as to feed their stomachs, accustomed to better fare, with only native bread and wild herbs without salt, often accompanied by river water, and even that wholesome drink sometimes failing. The earlier settlers of Darién, however, had hardened their bodies to enduring all evils and extreme starvation. Wherefore he humorously boasts that he kept a longer and harsher Lent than your Holiness, following the ordinance of our ancestors, commands to be observed. For he says that he and his companions spent four continuous years rarely full with the crops of the earth or fruits of trees; they used fish more rarely, meat most rarely of all. And he laments that things came to such a pass that, whenever they obtained them, they were forced to eat mangy dogs, muddy toads, and other such things in place of delicate feasts and splendid dishes. We have written of these things more extensively above. But by the earlier settlers of Darién I mean those who first attempted to settle the land under the leadership of Nicuesa and Ojeda, of whom few survived. Let us now dismiss these matters, and let Vasco be led back in victory across the lofty summits of the mountains.

Wherever the carriage approaches, which usually must proceed slowly enough, all eyes are turned toward it, and she has the joy of hearing from many sides: "Oh, how beautiful she is!" <note>original: "O quanto è bella!"</note>

Formerly, these ceremonial carriages are said to have been far more frequent and magnificent, and also more interesting on account of mythological and allegorical representations; in recent times, however, the nobility, for whatever reason it may be, lost within the whole crowd, seem to prefer enjoying the pleasure they still find in this celebration rather than distinguishing themselves before others.

The further the Carnival progresses, the more merry the carriages look.

Even serious persons, who sit unmasked in the carriages, allow their coachmen and servants to mask themselves. The coachmen mostly choose women's attire, and during the final days, only women seem to be driving the horses. They are often decently, even charmingly dressed; on the other hand, a broad, ugly fellow in entirely modern finery, with a high coiffure and feathers, presents a great caricature; and just as those beauties had their praises to hear, so he must submit to someone walking right up to his face and shouting to him: "Oh my brother, what an ugly whore you are!" <note>original: "O fratello mio, che brutta puttana sei!"</note>

Usually, when the coachman meets one or two of his female friends in the crowd, he does them the service of lifting them up onto the box. These women then usually sit at his side in men's clothing, and often the dainty <term>Pulcinella</term> <gloss>Punch, a standard comic figure of Italian street theatre</gloss> legs, with small feet and high heels, dangle playfully around the heads of the passers-by.

The servants do the same, taking their male and female friends onto the back of the carriages, and nothing is wanting except that they might also, as on English stagecoaches, sit atop the luggage box.

The masters and mistresses themselves seem pleased to see their carriages thoroughly packed; everything during these days is permitted and deemed proper.

Since writing the above Excursus, the writer has found
in the late Rev. J. L. Wilson’s book, *Western Africa*, which has
already been several times quoted from, the following passage :
> “Mixed up with these pagan notions and customs, there
are many obvious traces of Judaism, both in Northern and
Southern Guinea ; and in the latter some undoubted traces
of a corrupted form of Christianity, which have probably
travelled across the continent from ancient Ethiopia, where
Christianity was once firmly established.” He instances also
“bloody sacrifices, with the sprinkling of blood upon their
altars and door-posts, the formal and ceremonial observance
of new moons, etc.” ^1
